title: start with the person in the mirror
hook: start with the person in the mirror

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: thoughts. Your line: let it pass. Did one loud thought show up sounding very sure of itself? Did you let it pass, even once? Day eight, and week two begins.

A friend burns the dinner. Misses a deadline. Says the wrong thing at the wrong moment. What comes out of your mouth? Usually something like: hey, it happens, you're tired, it's fine. Now flip it. You burn the dinner. What does the voice inside say then? Sometimes it's a voice nobody would be allowed to use on a friend. Idiot. Of course you did. Typical. Week two is about how we treat people. And one old tradition insists you start with the person in the mirror. Today's word is kindness.
screen: `WHAT YOU SAY TO A FRIEND.` → `WHAT YOU SAY TO YOURSELF.` → `START WITH THE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: In the early Buddhist teachings there's a word, metta. It's usually translated loving-kindness, but it comes from the Pali word for friend. Metta is friendliness: wanting good for someone the way a friend does. A short discourse called the Metta Sutta describes it with a picture: the way a mother would protect her only child with her own life, a person can grow a heart like that toward every living being, without limit. Here's the surprise. The Buddhist teacher Buddhaghosa wrote a long guide to meditation, the Path of Purification, and when he explains how to practice metta, he says not to start with everyone. Start with yourself. Wish yourself well first, with phrases like may I be happy, may I be free from trouble. Then extend it outward: to someone dear, to someone neutral, and eventually to someone difficult. His reasoning is plain. You know from the inside that you want to be happy. That makes you the example: everyone else wants the same. Remember day four, and the line from Leviticus: "love thy neighbour as thyself." Those last two words carry a quiet assumption, that there's some care for yourself to measure by. And modern research points somewhere similar. The psychologist Kristin Neff studies what she calls self-compassion: treating your own failures the way you'd treat a friend's. A common worry is that being kind to yourself will make you lazy. Some of this research points the other way: in one set of studies, people nudged to be gentler about a mistake were more willing to own it, and put more effort into doing better. Kindness isn't a reward for getting it right. It's where you start.
screen: `METTA: THE FRIEND WORD.` · `START WITH YOURSELF, THEN OUTWARD.` · `AS THYSELF.` · `GENTLE WITH MISTAKES, MORE LIKELY TO TRY.` · then, large: `KINDNESS IS WHERE YOU START.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then picture yourself the way a good friend might see you right now: tired, trying, doing your best with the day you've had. On each breath out, say quietly inside: may I be at ease. That's all. If it feels strange or even a little silly, that's normal. Say it anyway. The bell holds the time.
Kindness. Wanting good for someone the way a friend does, starting with the one in the mirror. Eighth word.
Your line: may I be at ease. Today, the next time you catch the harsh voice inside after a mistake, stop and ask what you'd say to a friend. Then say that to yourself. Day eight.

screen: `DAY 8 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THREE THINGS, OUT LOUD, BADLY.`

howItsDone: In Buddhist loving-kindness (metta) meditation, practitioners often begin by silently wishing themselves well with a few short phrases, then extend the same wishes to a friend, a stranger, a difficult person and finally all beings.

fork.setup: you're learning metta from Buddhaghosa's guide. who do you wish well first?
options: someone difficult, to get the hard part over.

original.note: Pali, from the Buddhist tradition: friendliness, loving-kindness. It comes from mitta, friend (Sanskrit maitrī).

trapdoor: what you thought: being nice to other people.
what it means: wanting good for someone the way a friend does, starting with yourself.
what a scholar hears: mettā, from mitta, friend, as the Visuddhimagga itself explains it; Buddhaghosa begins the practice with oneself, as the example, before extending it outward.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (development of loving-kindness, beginning with oneself)
Kristin Neff, research on self-compassion (e.g. Neff 2003; Breines & Chen 2012)

notes: Mettā from mitta (friend): standard etymology; confirm.
Metta Sutta's mother-and-only-child image is paraphrased (Sutta Nipata 149).

Visuddhimagga IX: Buddhaghosa says to develop loving-kindness first toward oneself ('May I be happy and free from suffering'), then a dear person, a neutral person, a hostile person. 'About fifteen hundred years ago' dates him to the 5th century CE; confirm.
The Leviticus observation ('as thyself' assumes some care for oneself) is framed as a reader's observation, not a Jewish teaching; a Jewish Keeper may want to review.
Self-compassion findings (e.g. Breines & Chen 2012: self-compassion increased motivation to improve after failure) are summarized loosely; confirm wording 'tends to go the other way'.
Practice words 'may I be at ease' are a traditional-style metta phrase given as the day's carry, not a new prayer.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Think about' or says 'for a lot of us'; cut 'about fifteen hundred years ago' (no date in the cited text); Buddhaghosa's reason was misattributed ('it's hard to hand someone a thing you've never held' is not his) and now follows Visuddhimagga IX: oneself as the example, since one knows one wants happiness (speech, fork reveal, trapdoor); sequence now 'someone dear' as in the text; Neff findings narrowed to 'one set of studies' (Breines & Chen 2012) instead of 'her studies and others... tends to'; 'has spent years' cut. Metta-from-mitta kept because the Visuddhimagga (IX.93) gives that derivation itself.
